memory_update.text: AI theme should be treated as an infrastructure stack: cloud demand -> accelerators/HBM/packaging -> foundry/equipment -> networking/optics -> data-center power/cooling/grid -> enterprise software monetization.
HBM and advanced packaging are likely priority chokepoint nodes because AI accelerator availability depends on memory bandwidth and dense package integration, not only GPU die supply.
Data-center power, cooling, grid interconnection, and site infrastructure should be covered as a first-class AI node, not as a secondary utility afterthought.
AI networking and optical interconnect deserve separate coverage because cluster scale increases bandwidth, latency, optics, switching, and cabling constraints.
Need Layer 1B evidence expansion with filing-level capex extraction, latest earnings calls, supplier backlog data, regional power-market checks, and valuation/pricing screens.

summary: AI should be decomposed as a multi-layer infrastructure buildout rather than a single semiconductor or software story. The highest-quality first-pass funnel separates demand from hyperscaler and enterprise AI workloads, then maps the physical chokepoints: accelerators, HBM, advanced packaging, leading-edge foundry capacity, AI networking, data-center power/cooling/grid interconnection, and software/data-layer monetization. Layer 1A conclusion: the theme’s strongest bottleneck candidates are not only GPUs, but the constrained layers that determine whether compute can be installed, connected, powered, cooled, and monetized.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: If hyperscaler AI revenue and utilization keep rising, capex remains the primary demand engine; if utilization, enterprise adoption, or model ROI disappoints, the whole upstream chain faces overbuild risk.

Prioritize companies with disclosed AI backlog, contracted capacity, high utilization, and pass-through economics rather than generic AI branding.

demand_drivers: Hyperscaler AI infrastructure capex for cloud training, inference, foundation models, search, recommendation, coding assistants, enterprise copilots, and AI agents.
Enterprise migration from experimentation to production AI workloads, increasing demand for cloud compute, data governance, security, inference serving, model orchestration, and workflow automation.
Sovereign AI and national AI infrastructure programs that increase demand for local data centers, power capacity, networking, and secure semiconductor supply.
Inference growth as AI is embedded into consumer apps, enterprise software, advertising systems, industrial automation, robotics, defense, healthcare, and financial services.
Model scaling and multimodal workloads that increase memory bandwidth, interconnect bandwidth, power density, and cooling intensity per rack.
theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Start broad and avoid single-ticker anchoring. Build the public universe by supply-chain node: (1) cloud/hyperscaler capex issuers and AI model/platform companies; (2) accelerators, custom ASICs, HBM, foundry, EDA/IP, semiconductor equipment, substrates, advanced packaging, and test; (3) AI networking including Ethernet switches, NICs, optical modules, DSPs, lasers, and data-center cabling; (4) data-center physical infrastructure including power equipment, switchgear, transformers, UPS, cooling, liquid cooling, thermal materials, engineering/construction, REITs, utilities, grid services, gas turbines, nuclear, uranium/fuel cycle, and renewables/storage; (5) software and automation platforms with measurable AI revenue, usage, retention, and margin evidence. For each candidate, verify revenue exposure, capacity, customer qualification, backlog/orders, gross margin durability, capex intensity, and whether the market is already pricing the bottleneck.
supply_side_constraints: HBM supply is structurally concentrated among three memory suppliers and requires advanced stacking, TSV, testing, and packaging capacity.
Advanced packaging, especially CoWoS-like 2.5D integration and related substrates/interposers, can limit AI accelerator shipment even when logic wafers are available.
Leading-edge foundry capacity at advanced process nodes remains difficult to add quickly because of equipment lead times, yield learning, and customer qualification cycles.
AI networking bottlenecks can shift between Ethernet switching, custom ASICs, optical modules, DSPs, coherent optics, lasers, and high-speed copper/optical interconnects.
Data-center power availability, grid interconnection queues, transformers, switchgear, backup power, thermal management, and water constraints can delay compute deployment.
Software monetization may lag infrastructure spending if enterprises fail to convert AI pilots into durable productivity, revenue, or margin gains.
